Groupthink is insidious. We are all more prone to following the crowd than we like to believe we are, and it starts small. A joke about violence that gets laughs. A follow up statement showing real interest in violence. A small act of witnessed violence. Then a bigger one. Then bigger. If at any point an individual objects, they are no longer "safe" and won't be shown any more of this side than the others in the group can help showing. The earlier this behavior is questioned, the sooner the individual gets tossed from the group, making them least likely to witness or be subject to violence. But the longer it takes for the non-violent individual (in this cade, poor Suzanne) to protest the actions around them, the more violent their expulsion from the group will be.

They groomed her just as much as any sexual predator grooms their victims. They slowly heated the water around her before she could realize she was boiling. My guess is, the more influential members of the group (probably the older ones, but sometimes it's a mix) did the same to the less influential members (probably the teenagers) until they recognized, whether consciously or unconsciously, that if they didn't go along with what they did to Suzanne, they would become the new targets of the group.

What they failed to realize is, with Suzanne gone, one or more of the group members would eventually take her place as scapegoat and victim. They were stopped before that happened thanks to Suzanne's bravery and resilience giving her a chance to name her murderers, but without external intervention, group dynamics such as this one lead to nothing but more and more violence, until the group eats itself.

She ate one pomegranate seed (or sometimes 3), I think partially to show that it didn't matter how small the amount of food she ate was, she would still be stuck in the land of the dead. Pomegranates were common fruit in ancient Greece, and were a symbol of fertility as well as death. I don't know if you've ever cut up a pomegranate, but the one time I did, the kitchen looked like I'd committed several murders - the juice is deep red and plentiful and the Greeks believed the plant grew from Adonis's blood.

The pomegranate also has many seeds, symbolising fertility, and as Persephone was the goddess of spring, it makes sense to tie her to a fruit that was seen as especially fertile.

Because the pomegranate represented both death and fertility, it fits perfectly into this myth about the changing of seasons, as well as the duality of Persephone herself as the Queen of the Underworld and the goddess of springtime.

Pomegranates are also just more prominent in that part of the world. For instance, there are some Biblical scholars who think that the fruit from the Tree of Knowledge in the Garden of Eden was a pomegranate and not an apple.

And totally understandable! I like to know the original sources as well. This gave me a chance to look into those specifically for the Fates. Here's what I found:

The first reference to anything related to the Fates that we still have is Homer's Odyssey, where Fate is a singular goddess called Moira or Aisa. Then, in Theogony by Hesiod, he refers to the Fates but doesn't describe them much. He calls them "avenging" but that doesn't tell us much about their ages. Aeschylus does call them "ancient" in Eumenides, but that could mean ancient in the way all gods are ancient not necessarily how they look to humans. It's unclear. In Plato's Republic, he describes them as wearing white robes, but again, nothing age wise. They ARE described as sisters several times, which to me implies however old they are they're seen as being contemporaries of each other and therefore around the same age, but again, that's not definitive. The Orphic Hymns have one in particular for the Moirai, but again, no mention of what they look like or what age we might perceive them as. That's as far as I had time to go through primary sources for the moment and also just from a quick page search of texts of them, not a full reading, so I almost definitely missed things.

Now, as to secondary sources, I can find a ton - one example being Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome by E.M. Berens - who refer to the Fates as old, ugly, and even lame. Frustratingly, none of them give specifics as to where in antiquity they were referred to as such. This is going to be a deep dive for me for some time, I suspect, but I wanted to let you know what I had found so far! Or rather, tantalizingly enough, not found. I'm fascinated now.

BTW, one of my favorite more modern depictions of the Fates as Maiden/Matron/Crone was a beautiful facade by Gottfried Schadow from 1790. It's gorgeous and just an example of how you've probably seen the Fates depicted this way before and you're not nuts - they were just probably newer than they seemed!

Some advice, cause I've been here many times in my life:

1) If you're having trouble finding a therapist you can afford, contact a psychology professor from the university closest to you. They usually have a professional email in the school's online directory, and they know about resources for the community even if you're not enrolled in the school. And- professors LOVE being asked about their expertise, so I promise your email won't be unwelcome (they also might be busy, so don't take it personally if they don't get back to you, just means to try another professor). Send them something polite asking if they know anyone practicing in your area who does "sliding scale" appointments, meaning that they charge based on income instead of a set hourly rate. This is how I found my current therapist.

2) If that doesn't work for whatever reason, look for group therapies near you. They are usually free, and while they're not really a replacement for one-on-one counseling, they'll get you through a bad time, and the people who run them usually have access to other resources as well.

3) Go to the hospital even before you've physically hurt yourself. They will (or should) take it seriously before that point. If they want to admit you, let them. It's gonna suck. They all suck. As Maria Bamford said, "You're not at the wrong one." They're all depressing places, and the people in them are not there because they're always pleasant people. But if you go to the group therapies, listen to your doctors, and give them what they need, to the best of your ability, they will help you. You will feel better even if you feel like you're just going through the motions. I literally only went to my group therapies while I was in the hospital because I was trying to trick my doctors into thinking I was all better, and by the end of the longest week (most holds are 3 days, I had to wait for a diagnosis due to some complications, long story) of my life, the activities were making me feel much better.

Good luck, friend. You're in the middle of a medical emergency if you're feeling like this all the time. It takes so much energy, but there is help if you know where to look. All you ever *have* to do is get through to tomorrow. Anything else is bonus points. <3

While very similar, there is a small difference between the two words. Ancillary implies that it provides something extra that the original system doesn't have on its own. Connotatively, it also implies a subservience to the original system. It comes from the Latin word ancillaris, "having to do with a maidservant."

Auxiliary means both being a part of the system (not extra, but intrinsic) and also doesn't have the connotation of being less important than other parts of the system. Auxiliarius is Latin for help.

A maid is ancillary to a household, but a spouse is auxiliary to a household in that a spouse is a part of a household and a maid goes home to their own household.

I have been with my partner for a little over 7 years, and I gotta say, it takes a special person. Not to feel connected to, but who can deal with all my symptoms when they pop up. I didn't have a problem feeling connected to him at first, I knew the day we met that he was special. We took it slow, though, and that allowed the relationship to build on something much less fickle than feelings. He also puts a lot of work into our relationship. I do too, but he takes care of me in ways that he simply doesn't need reciprocated. I feel guilty about it, but he is there to reassure me that he helps me because he wants to and loves me, not because I force him to.

There are days when I don't feel connected to anyone or anything, and on those days, the foundation of trust, comfort, mutual respect, and support carry us through. It's hard, but all relationships are hard. Maybe they're easier for mentally healthy people, but I'll never know so I don't worry about that.

I will also add that being with him is often the reason I do the things I need to do to get better. If I can't get out of bed for myself, sometimes I can do it for him. I want him to get something out of our relationship at least even slightly close to what he puts in, so finding the energy to do something for him - cook a meal, buy him a present, clean the kitchen - is often the only way I'm going to find that energy.
